signals.title: Building on Nemotron 3.5 Parse: Open Data, Fine-Tuning, and Faster Inference
signals.excerpt:
Published November 26, 2026 

We recently released NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Parse, a compact document model that turns page images into structured data for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and agents.

Now we’re building on that release with synthetic training datasets, a fine-tuning recipe, and a DFlash2 speculator for faster inference. We’re also sharing how we trained Parse 3.5: first teaching document understanding through supervised fine-tuning, then using reinforcement learning to improve accuracy, consistency, and reliable completion.

## What Parse 3.5 produces 

Parse extracts content from pages of documents into reading order, assigns content classes such as headings, paragraphs, tables, and charts, and returns bounding boxes that locate the content. Tables and charts become structured records that can power downstream document processing applications.

...

This latest version of Parse significantly extends its ability to read charts and tables, especially in more difficult and ambiguous cases. For example, bar charts or other plots that do not have any marked numeric values. The model is able to infer values by looking at the axes and height of the bar to derive these. Tables can be especially tricky because the structure is so meaningful, a shifted row or column can totally change the interpretation and meaning. These advancements have been largely powered by synthetic data generation, rendering variations of charts and tables with known ground truth and then training our model to reverse this process.

We are open-sourcing three datasets used in the Parse 3.5 training:

- Synthetic Charts V1 — 9.98M examples: rendered charts and structured annotations for learning categories, series, and numerical values.
- Synthetic Tables V1 — 1M examples: rendered HTML tables with targets that preserve rows, columns, headers, and cell relationships.
- OCR Synthetic Multilingual v2 — 7.9M examples: synthetic document pages with Parse-format targets across varied fonts and layouts, for multilingual OCR and structured page reading.

Each release includes images, annotations, generation documentation, and the training format. Use these pairs to fine-tune document models or create new variations for a target document type or language.

...

## SFT teaches the capability; RLVR improves consistency 

We trained Parse 3.5 with two phases of training. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) spanning text, layout, tables, charts, and multilingual documents. Learning to predict structured targets established the general capability of reading a page and representing its contents.

We then continued with reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). Rewards check the quality of sampled extractions. For example, a chart extraction can earn a better reward for recovering the correct series and values, producing a usable structure, and finishing without repeatedly generating the same content.

A difficult page can have several valid representations. These checks give the model flexibility to find a correct answer without prescribing one exact token sequence, while discouraging looping and unfinished output.

Figure 3. A controlled comparison of SFT and GRPO with matched evaluation settings. These are development checkpoints, separate from the final released model. Loop counts use a repetition check. Methods.

The matched comparison shows the benefit: loop-flagged outputs fall from 126 to 29 pages—about 77% fewer—and outputs reaching the 9,000-token limit fall from 185 to 35. Overall score improves from 66.24 to 71.38, including +5.18 points in tables and +4.15 in charts.

## Faster inference through architecture and DFlash2 

A parser must generate substantial text and structure for every page. Alongside the training work, we optimized how Parse 3.5 processes images and decodes those outputs.

| Component | Parse 2.0 | Parse 3.5 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Page preprocessing | Fixed 2048 × 1664 canvas | NaViT dynamic rectangular inputs |
| Image-to-text connection | Encoder–decoder cross-attention | Compressed visual tokens as a causal prefix |
| Decoder self-attention | Multi-head attention | GQA-8: 16 query heads, 8 key/value heads |
| Speculative decoding | | One-token lookahead (MTP); optional DFlash2 |

NaViT preprocessing adapts the input shape to the page. A visual adapter compresses the image sequence, and the text decoder consumes it as a prefix, replacing encoder–decoder cross-attention. Grouped-query attention with eight key/value heads (GQA-8) reduces the decoder’s attention-cache memory.

The built-in multi-token prediction (MTP) head supplies one-token lookahead. Our DFlash2 speculator goes further: a small draft model proposes up to 32 tokens ahead, and Parse verifies the proposals together. In the measured 32-token configuration, it averages about 14 accepted draft tokens, or roughly 15 output tokens of progress per verification step including the target token.

Figure 4. Native single-pass throughput on one H200, BF16, using the same 2,078 pages. Parse 2.0 uses one trial per point; Parse 3.5 shows three-trial medians. Arrows show the gain from Parse 3.5 base to DFlash2. Measurement details.

In the native single-pass benchmark on one H200 in BF16, DFlash2 increased throughput 7.62× at concurrency 1 and 1.52× at concurrency 512, compared with Parse 3.5 with speculative decoding disabled. At 512, Parse 3.5 reaches 13.48 pages/s without speculation and 20.44 pages/s with DFlash2, versus 2.98 for Parse 2.0. Those are 4.53× and 6.86× the Parse 2.0 throughput, respectively.

Fast parsing gives us room to revisit difficult regions.

...

In the published reference evaluation, double and triple pass add 2.18 and 2.46 ParseBench points over single pass.

On SemiAnalysis InferenceX's AgentX benchmark, TokenSpeed establishes a new measured throughput–interactivity frontier for Muse Spark Open on AMD Instinct™ MI355X GPUs, from latency-first serving on eight GPUs to throughput-first serving on four. The result comes from co-designing expert placement, multi-GPU communication, fused Gluon kernels and agent-aware scheduling as one serving system.¹

## Highlights

- A new MI355X frontier. TokenSpeed is ahead of the published baseline on both interactivity and total throughput per GPU at all six matched operating points: by 2.5–30% on interactivity and by 0.5–13% on throughput.¹

Benchmark numbers in these highlights: SemiAnalysis InferenceX™, AgentX. They are SemiAnalysis’s own testing, separate from AMD internal measurements.¹

signals.title: Building a RAG System That Says "I Don't Know": Self-Correcting RAG with Llama 3.1 and LangGraph - DEV Community
signals.excerpt:
Abuzar Zulfiqar
Posted on Nov 26 • Originally published at abuzar18.github.io • AI-assisted
# Building a RAG System That Says "I Don't Know": Self-Correcting RAG with Llama 3.1 and LangGraph
Most RAG demos have the same flaw: ask them something the documents never mention, and they answer anyway, confidently and wrongly. In a demo that is a curiosity. In production it is how a support bot invents a refund policy.
I built Llama Agentic RAG around the opposite rule: **an answer must be supported by cited sources, or the system says "I don't know."** It runs fully locally on Llama 3.1 8B through Ollama, which fits in 8 GB of VRAM, so private documents never leave the machine.
This post walks through the design and the choices that made it work on a small model.
## The workflow
The pipeline is a LangGraph state machine with five stages:
1. **Retrieve** the top-k chunks from a vector index. Every chunk has a stable id such as `handbook.md#3`, so citations stay traceable.
2. **Grade** each chunk for relevance with the LLM before anything is generated. Off-topic context never reaches the answer.
3. **Rewrite** the query once if no chunk is relevant. Vague questions often recover here; if they don't, the graph refuses.
4. **Generate** an answer only from the numbered context, citing `[n]` after each claim.
5. **Check groundedness**: a judge prompt verifies the answer against the context. An unsupported answer is replaced by a refusal.
The key idea is that hallucinations become refusals, not wrong answers. A refusal is annoying; a confident wrong answer is expensive.
## Making it work on an 8B model
Large models forgive sloppy prompts. Small models don't, so a few details mattered more than any framework choice:
* **One-word verdicts.** Llama 3.1 8B is unreliable with complex JSON schemas, so the grading and groundedness prompts ask for `yes` or `no`, and parsing is tolerant of extra words.
* **Strip reasoning tags.** If you swap in a reasoning model, its ` ` blocks are removed before parsing.
* **Citations are enforced, not requested.** An answer without valid `[n]` citations is treated as ungrounded, even if it sounds right.
* **Config over code.** Every model, path and threshold is an environment variable, so trying another Ollama model is a one-line change.
## Measure the refusals
A RAG system that never says "I don't know" isn't production-ready, so the evaluation set deliberately includes unanswerable questions. The harness reports:
|Metric|What it tells you|
|Retrieval hit rate|Did we retrieve an expected source for answerable questions?|
|Citation precision|Do cited chunks come from expected sources?|
|Refusal accuracy|Were unanswerable questions correctly refused?|
|False-refusal rate|Were answerable questions wrongly refused?|
|Judge correctness|LLM-as-judge score against a reference answer|
|p50 / p95 latency|What does it cost the user in time?|
Refusal accuracy and false-refusal rate pull against each other, which is exactly why you need both. Tighten the groundedness check and refusals get safer while false refusals rise. The numbers make that trade-off visible instead of a matter of opinion.
Treat prompt and model changes like code changes: they ship only if the evals hold.
## Tests that don't need a GPU
CI runs the full graph with scripted fake LLM replies and deterministic embeddings. That covers the happy path, query rewrite, refusal, ungrounded answers, missing citations and reasoning-tag stripping, all without a model or a GPU. It is the cheapest way to keep a graph's control flow honest as it grows.
## Use it from Claude with MCP
The same graph is exposed as an MCP tool, `ask\_documents`, so Claude Desktop, Claude Code or any MCP client can query your documents and get cited answers back. The FastAPI service exposes `/ask`, `/ingest` and `/health` for everything else.
## What's next
The roadmap is the usual path from reference to production: hybrid retrieval with BM25 and a cross-encoder reranker, a persistent vector database such as pgvector or Qdrant, tracing with Langfuse, streaming, and PDF and DOCX ingestion.
The code is MIT-licensed: github.com/abuzar18/llama-agentic-rag. If you are building RAG for a team that can't afford confident wrong answers, I'd be glad to compare notes.

signals.title:
From Files to Cited Answers in One API Call: Managed Ingestion and SearchDocuments in Agent Retrieval
            
            
            - Google Developers Blog
signals.excerpt:
NOV. 24, 2026

 Yingxin Jiang Software Engineer 

 Kaz Sato Staff Developer Advocate 

A guide to the new managed ingestion and SearchDocuments features in Agent Retrieval, for searching PDFs, Office files, and videos without writing an ingestion pipeline.

Before an agent can answer a question about your PDFs, someone has to build the pipeline: parse every file, split it into chunks, embed each chunk, write the chunks to a vector database, and then learn that database's schema to query it. For video it gets harder: transcode the files, cut them into clips, embed the frames, and keep track of which second of which video each clip came from.

 Before: every step of the pipeline is custom code you write and maintain, separately for documents and for videos. 

Most of that code has nothing to do with your application. Two features recently added to Agent Retrieval (formerly Vector Search 2.0), now in Public Preview, take that work off your hands. Managed ingestion builds the pipeline for you: point a data store at files in Cloud Storage, and the service parses, segments, and embeds them with Gemini Embedding 2. SearchDocuments, the second new feature, then searches the data store with one API call and returns the matching passages with their page numbers or timestamps. In our tests, 18 Alphabet investor PDFs went from a public Cloud Storage bucket to searchable, page cited results in about 9 minutes, and 19 minutes of video became searchable by both visuals and spoken audio in 0.3 to 0.5 seconds per query, with no parsing, chunking, transcription, or embedding code.

This guide covers how to create a data store, import documents and videos, and search them with filters, reranking, and audio-aware video search.

### What Managed Ingestion and SearchDocuments Enable

 After: create separate data stores for documents (UNSTRUCTURED) and videos (VIDEO), point each at Cloud Storage, and search each with one SearchDocuments call that returns cited results. 

Pairing managed ingestion with SearchDocuments gives you several immediate benefits:

- No Ingestion Pipeline: Import PDF, DOCX, PPTX, XLSX, and TXT files, or MP4, MOV, WebM, MKV, and other video formats, straight from Cloud Storage. Parsing, segmentation, embedding, and the vector Collection and its schema are handled for you.
- Answers With Citations: Every result carries its source file URI and a page range for documents, or a start and end time for videos, so your agent can cite exactly where an answer came from.
- One Call to Search: SearchDocuments takes a data store and a text query. You don't pass a Collection name, a vector field, a task type, or output fields, and hybrid search (semantic + full-text) runs automatically for documents.
- Search What Was Said in Videos: Turn on audio embedding and a query matches the moment a speaker mentions a topic, even when the picture shows something else. No transcript or captions required.

...

### How It Works in Practice

1. Hybrid Retrieval: SearchDocuments runs a semantic search and a full-text search over the backing Collection and fuses the two result lists, so both paraphrased questions and exact terms match.
2. Segment-Level Results: Results are pages or chunks, not whole files. Several results can come from the same document, each with its own page range.
3. Optional Reranking: With reranking on, SearchDocuments retrieves more candidates than `top_k` and reorders them with the Ranking API, using the same `semantic-ranker-fast@latest` model as Agent Retrieval's `VertexRanker`.

signals.title: Improving AI efficiency with optimization | MIT Sloan
signals.excerpt:
## Optimization applied to model compression

Mazumder’s team develops large-scale optimization algorithms for AI model compression, the process of shrinking AI models so they use fewer resources. Say the mandate is to compress the model so it sacrifices 1% of accuracy compared with the original, uncompressed model. There will be disagreement as to what percentage of the model to compress to achieve that goal, he said.

Optimization helps teams decide what to remove and how much utility to retain within a given computing budget, Mazumder said, and provides everyone with a common language for weighing those trade-offs.

“The model optimization takes into account task-specific data, whether you care about industrial analytics or ranking a product,” as well as any compute-aware hardware constraints, he explained.

To that end, Mazumder and his team developed ADMM-Q, a procedure for quantizing LLMs, which he presented at the Conference on Language Modeling in October.

During his talk, Mazumder showed that an 8-billion-parameter AI model that was compressed with ADMM-Q answered a question noticeably faster than the uncompressed original. Compression can make serving a model one-and-a-half-times faster, he said, and has implications for both energy and GPU savings.

What sets ADMM-Q apart, he said, is accuracy: The research team found that models compressed with ADMM-Q retained more of the original model’s performance than those compressed with standard methods, especially when the model was made much smaller.

Ultimately, Mazumder said, his goal is to see whether it’s possible to design high-performing AI models while ensuring that they are resource-efficient.

signals.title: How to Optimize NVFP4 Attention on NVIDIA RTX Blackwell Through Register Recycling | NVIDIA Technical Blog
signals.excerpt:
Attention can be a major bottleneck when serving world foundation models, where long sequences make inference computationally demanding. On NVIDIA Hopper and NVIDIA Blackwell data center GPUs, FlashAttention3 and FlashAttention4 improve attention performance by overlapping matrix multiply-accumulate (MMA) operations through softmax within a thread block.

However, these hardware-specific pipelines cannot be applied directly to the NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Series (SM120), which uses a different Tensor Core architecture. For video generation models using BF16 inference, attention remains primarily MMA-bound on NVIDIA Blackwell RTX GPUs, while softmax is a major bottleneck in forward attention on Blackwell data center GPUs.

Introduced with NVIDIA Blackwell architecture, NVFP4 offers hardware-accelerated 4-bit matrix multiplication, enabling higher Tensor Core throughput and creating an opportunity to accelerate attention beyond BF16. But sustaining high throughput requires careful coordination of softmax, data movement, and intermediate storage. Dependencies between these stages can leave Tensor Cores idle, limiting how effectively the kernel uses the available compute.

This post explains how to accelerate NVFP4 attention on the SM120 architecture through register recycling and improved scheduling. By reclaiming score registers after the softmax outputs have been packed into NVFP4, the next tile’s matrix multiplication can overlap with remaining softmax work on the current tile. This creates a more efficient pipeline that reduces Tensor Core idle time and improves utilization without requiring a second full score buffer.

Reactor, a developer platform that provides global low-latency infrastructure and APIs for deploying and scaling real-time video, robotics, and world models, integrated this kernel in their production serving stack to serve real customer traffic and saw tremendous speedups. Their benchmarks are shared in this post.

...

Reactor integrated this NVFP4 attention kernel into its production serving infrastructure and used it to serve real customer traffic across several models. Table 2 shows the impact on end-to-end model inference latency on NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell.

Latency was measured for the complete model path per video chunk, full generation, or action prediction. The table specifies which attention operations use NVFP4; other attention operations and model weights remain BF16. The terms idle and moving refer to camera scenarios with the same NVFP4 coverage.

For the video-chunk and action-prediction benchmarks, the BF16 baseline uses native cuDNN attention. Timings include quantization, layout conversion, and decoded CPU-frame or action output, but exclude model loading, warmup, networking, queueing, and client pacing.

signals.title: Generalized Tensor Parallelism: Many Parallelisms, One Framework - NVIDIA Nemotron
signals.excerpt:
Published: November 24, 2026

Treating parameter re-materialization as a preprocessing step on one input of a GEMM improves compute-communication overlap, letting a 2T-parameter MoE train at 1,060 TFLOP/s per GPU on 12K GB300 GPUs.

...

All results are on NVIDIA GB300 GPUs in 72-GPU NVLink domains.

### 1,060 TFLOP/s per GPU on 12,288 GPUs

With GTP, an internal 2T-parameter MoE model (Internal-2T) trains at 1,060 TFLOP/s per GPU on 12,288 GB300 GPUs, or 13.0 EFLOP/s (13.0 × 10 18 floating-point operations per second) in total, with 8K sequences, Muon, and no pipeline parallelism. Weak-scaling efficiency from 4,096 to 12,288 GPUs is 98.2%.

### Faster than Megatron-FSDP, and the gap grows with scale

Across three MoE models at 256–1,024 GPUs, GTP achieves 1.05–1.55× the throughput of Megatron-FSDP with 4–16% lower per-GPU memory. GTP’s weak-scaling efficiency from 256 to 1,024 GPUs is about 98% on every model, compared with 79.3% and 86.7% for Megatron-FSDP on the DeepSeek-V4-Pro and Internal-2T proxies. Profiles show why: Megatron-FSDP’s exposed all-gather time in the backward pass grows with scale and varies from step to step as GPUs wait for the slowest GPU in each group, while GTP’s stays nearly flat.

...

### Faster than tuned 3D parallelism

On the DeepSeek-V4-Pro proxy, GTP achieves 1.27–1.31× the throughput of a tuned 3D-parallel recipe (TP, PP with virtual pipelining, and DP) at 256–1,024 GPUs. GTP spends some of its memory savings on larger microbatches here: at the same microbatch size it uses 11–13% less memory than 3D parallelism, while at the sizes that maximize each method’s throughput it uses 29–48% more.

The interesting part is where the time goes. Per-GPU compute is similar for both methods, but the pipeline’s last stage computes 20% more than the stage mean, and a pipeline runs at the speed of its slowest stage. The other stages spend the difference waiting: 29% of the first stage’s step, compared with an ideal pipeline bubble of 4.5%. GTP has no stages to balance, so its training step is 20% shorter, even though its weight all-gathers and gradient reduce-scatters expose 8% and 5% of the step.

signals.title: PrismML shrinks a 54 GB language model to 5.9 GB by reducing every weight to just three possible values
signals.excerpt:
Startup PrismML has released Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B, an updated version of its aggressively compressed language model. It's based on Qwen3.8-27B and takes up just 5.9 GB of memory, same as its predecessor. That's possible because of ternary quantization, where each weight can only be one of three values (−1, 0, or +1) instead of the usual 16-bit storage. At full precision, a model this size would need about 54 GB.

Bonsai 2.5 is designed to perform more reliably on agentic tasks that involve long chains of tool calls. It needs fewer passes and tokens than Bonsai 2, and it's less likely to get stuck in loops or spiral into drawn-out reasoning phases.

The benchmark numbers reflect the improvement. On SWE-bench Verified, the score jumps from 60.8 to 75.6 percent. The full Qwen model hits 80.6. On AppWorld, an agent benchmark, Bonsai leaps from 51.2 to 90.5, landing just behind the base model. On LiveCodeBench v6, the new version scores slightly lower than its predecessor.

On an RTX 4090, the model generates about 204 tokens per second using multi-token prediction. The weights are available under an Apache 2.0 license and run via llama.cpp on Nvidia and Intel GPUs, as well as through MLX on Mac, iPhone, and iPad.

signals.title: RL infrastructure at Microsoft AI | Microsoft AI
signals.excerpt:
For MAI Thinking 1, we prioritized numerical fidelity by retaining BF16 weights and KV caches throughout the sampler. Since MAI Base 2 is a much larger model, we selectively use MXFP8 for MoE weights and KV caches to accelerate rollouts while maintaining training stability. Figure 5 summarizes the precision choices in the sampler and learner.

MoE expert weights account for over 95% of the model’s parameters. Storing these weights in MXFP8 rather than BF16 nearly halves the sampler’s weight memory footprint, enabling a smaller expert-parallel (EP) degree and fewer GPUs per sampler replica. In our experiments, performing the expert matrix multiplications in MXFP8 produced larger sampler–learner log-probability discrepancies than dequantizing the MXFP8 weights to BF16 and multiplying them with BF16 activations. We therefore store MoE weights in MXFP8 but dequantize them to BF16 for computation. This retains most of the speed benefits while keeping the sampler closer to the learner. To improve training stability, we reproduce the sampler’s weight quantization in the learner by quantizing MoE weights to MXFP8 and immediately dequantizing them to BF16 for computation.

We apply the same separation of storage and compute precision to the sampler’s global-attention KV cache. Within the attention kernel, quantized KV entries are dequantized to BF16 for computation. The learner applies corresponding KV fake quantization to reproduce the sampler’s quantization effects. The smaller KV cache footprint supports longer sequences and higher rollout concurrency, while reducing the need to offload KV entries or retract requests under memory pressure.

MAI Base 2 mixes local and global attention layers at a ratio of 5:1, and our ablations showed that quantizing both local- and global-attention KV caches introduced substantially larger sampler–learner log-probability discrepancies than quantizing global-attention KV caches alone. We therefore retain BF16 KV caches for local-attention, and, as a numerical precaution, for the final three global attention layers. All other global-attention layers use MXFP8 storage. The resulting KV cache configuration accommodates approximately 67% more global-context tokens than the BF16 KV cache configuration, while maintaining roughly the same local-attention cache capacity.

signals.title: MixMoMo Tests 80-Billion-Parameter Generative AI on Smartphones Using Both GPU and NPU | Joho no Todai
signals.excerpt:
Researchers have demonstrated large generative AI models on smartphones with 16GB of memory. MixMoMo adjusts weight-quantization precision based on the input and distributes computation between the GPU and NPU to balance response quality with generation speed.

...

Researchers from Peking University and Tianjin University in China have published a paper on MixMoMo, a generative AI inference system for smartphones. The original title is MixMoMo: Accelerating Extra–Large MoE Inference with Mixed–Precision GPU–NPU Execution on Mobile Devices.

The OnePlus 15 used in the experiments had a Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5, 16GB of memory, and 256GB of UFS 4.1 storage. The OnePlus 13 system used a Snapdragon 8 Elite, 24GB of memory, and 1TB of UFS 4.0 storage.

The three AI models tested were Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B, Kimi-Linear-48B-A3B, and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B. Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B has 80 billion total parameters, but its developer's specifications say only 3 billion parameters are active during inference.

This is possible because of a design called mixture of experts (MoE), which selects the necessary computational components, or experts, from multiple components in the model according to the input. A Qwen3-Next MoE layer uses 10 of 512 available experts.

...

But loading the selected experts' weights from storage into memory as needed makes it possible to perform inference with limited memory.

...

## Where precision can be reduced depends on the input

Quantization, which represents model weights with fewer bits, is used to reduce storage and memory consumption. Lowering precision reduces capacity requirements, but it can also affect the AI's answers.

The team found that quantization can substantially change the model's final output even when an expert receives only a small weight in the combined output. The effect on the final output varies with the combination of quantization errors in the weights and the data entering the expert.

MixMoMo measures the effect of quantizing each expert on the final output in advance. During actual inference, it combines the incoming data values with those premeasured results to estimate the risk of reducing precision.

The available precisions are nominally 2-bit, 4-bit, 8-bit, and FP16, or 16-bit floating point. MixMoMo begins by assigning low precision, then raises the precision of the necessary experts until the estimated risk falls within an acceptable range. Its distinguishing feature is that it selects precision according to the input.

Weights at different precisions use a common representation in storage and are loaded at the precision required for inference. This design also limits the additional storage capacity that would otherwise result from using multiple precisions.

## Reducing GPU and NPU wait times

GPUs and NPUs, processors specialized for AI operations, differ in the calculations and data handling they perform well. In the team's comparison, simply assigning experts according to the processing capacity of each processor could be slower than using the NPU alone for some combinations of quantization precision.

When both processors calculate in parallel, combining the results requires waiting for the slower one to finish.

MixMoMo therefore measures GPU and NPU execution times in advance for different precisions and numbers of experts. It accounts for loading weights, converting them into the format needed for computation, performing the calculation, and transferring data, then chooses the split predicted to complete expert processing in the shortest time during inference.

The researchers also modified processing inside the NPU. On the tested GPU, low-precision weights can be unpacked and dequantized—converted into the numerical values used for computation—with the matrix calculation combined into a single operation. On the tested NPU, quantized weights are converted to FP16 before matrix calculations are performed.

Previously, each divided block of weights required preparation for unpacking and dequantization. MixMoMo processes compatible blocks together to use the NPU's parallel-computing capability. It also groups work by precision at each computation stage, reducing the overhead from execution commands and synchronization on the NPU.

The implementation uses the existing generative AI inference engine llama.cpp. The team added about 8,000 lines of C/C++ code for OpenCL, Qualcomm's Hexagon HTP, and other components.

## What contributed to the speedup?

The researchers compared performance on five types of datasets: math problems, code generation, news summarization, knowledge questions, and dialogue. All mixed-precision methods used an average expert quantization precision of 4 bits, and the team measured processing time per output token, the unit into which text is divided for processing.

MixMoMo Smartphone Performance Evaluation

| Generation-speed comparison with existing methods (two devices, five tasks; mixed precision averages 4 bits) | | | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| AI model | | Vs. uniform 4-bit | Vs. best mixed-precision method |
| Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B | | 3.61x | 1.50x |
| Kimi-Linear-48B-A3B | | 4.06x | 1.61x |
| Qwen3.6-35B-A3B | | 3.49x | 1.48x |
| Three-model average | | 3.72x | 1.53x |
| Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B: Added Features and Generation Speed | | | |
| Added features (cumulative) | | GSM8K ms/token | Three-task average |
| Uniform 4-bit (baseline) | | 1111.11 | 1.00x |
| + Quantization-precision control | | 1123.59 | 1.01x |
| + GPU-NPU distribution | | 498.26 | 2.32x |
| + Parallel NPU dequantization and processing integration | | 327.87 | 3.61x |
| Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B: Answer Quality | | | |
| Method | GSM8K accuracy | HumanEval Pass@1 | MMLU-Pro Accuracy |
| FP16 | 84.53% | 92.12% | 76.35% |
| Uniform 4-bit | 80.46% | 87.94% | 71.48% |
| MixMoMo | 84.48% | 92.00% | 75.87% |

The paper reports an average token-generation speed across the three models that was 3.72x that of uniform 4-bit quantization (Q4_0). It was an average of 1.53x the fastest existing mixed-precision method for each model. Compared with uniform 4-bit quantization, Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B was 3.61x faster, Kimi-Linear-48B-A3B was 4.06x faster, and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B was 3.49x faster.

For Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B, the team also conducted tests on three tasks while adding each feature in stages. Adding only quantization-precision control produced an average speed of 1.01x that of uniform 4-bit quantization. Adding GPU-NPU work distribution raised it to 2.32x, while also adding parallel NPU dequantization and integration of processing by precision brought it to 3.61x.

On GSM8K, a benchmark of mathematical word problems, uniform 4-bit quantization required 1,111.11 milliseconds per output token, while MixMoMo with all features enabled required 327.87 milliseconds. That is an improvement from about 0.90 tokens per second to about 3.05 tokens per second.

The researchers also measured answer quality for MixMoMo with quantization-precision control. On GSM8K, Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B achieved 84.53% accuracy with FP16, 80.46% with uniform 4-bit quantization, and 84.48% with MixMoMo. On HumanEval, a set of programming tasks used to assess code generation, Pass@1—the probability that a single generated answer passes the tests—was 92.12% for FP16, 87.94% for uniform 4-bit quantization, and 92.00% for MixMoMo.

The quality comparison and staged speed measurements show that precision control and acceleration play different roles. Varying precision limits quality degradation from quantization, while improving data preparation and computation assignment increases speed. The research is notable for combining the effects of both approaches.

signals.title: Mellum2.1 Instruct Is Out, Bringing Faster Answers for Coding Agents - The JetBrains Blog
signals.excerpt:
In October, we released Mellum2.1 Thinking, an open 12B mixture-of-experts model with 2.5B active parameters, trained to work as a coding agent. Today, we are releasing its sibling, Mellum2.1 Instruct. It is built on the same architecture and trained identically, but it gives straight answers without including its chain of thought.

What sets Mellum2.1 apart from Mellum2 is its post-training phase: large-scale reinforcement learning on repository-level tasks in real environments, built on NVIDIA NeMo open-source training libraries – NeMo RL and NeMo Megatron-Bridge for efficient large-scale distributed training.

As promised, this October we released the multi-token prediction (MTP) head for Mellum2.1 Thinking, making token generation up to 1.8x faster. Mellum2.1 Instruct is released together with its MTP head.

## Why an Instruct model, and when to use it

Reasoning models, such as Mellum2.1 Thinking, are a good fit for tasks that require a step-by-step approach, like finding the root cause of a failing test. But much of a coding agent’s work is simpler, like a small fix, a command to run, or a question about the code. In these cases, reasoning adds time and computing resources without adding quality.

This is especially true when the model runs locally – every extra thinking token adds to the time you’re waiting. After the Thinking release, we received many requests from the local-inference community for a more concise model for moderately hard tasks.

That is where Mellum2.1 Instruct fits in – either on its own or as the fast worker next to a stronger model. On agentic coding tasks, it generates about half as many tokens as the Thinking variant and performs almost as well on SWE-bench Verified. On hard algorithmic and math problems, such as those in LiveCodeBench and AIME, thinking is crucial, and so Mellum2.1 Thinking remains the better choice.

 

 

## Performance on benchmarks

We compared Mellum2.1 Instruct with its predecessor, Mellum2 Instruct, and two open models in the same class, Qwen3.5 9B and Gemma 4 E4B, both with thinking turned off.

The biggest gain is on the agentic benchmark SWE-bench Verified, where the score doubled compared with the previous Instruct release. The new training also improved code generation, where Mellum2.1 Instruct now leads the group, and multi-step tool use, where it is level with Qwen3.5 9B.

Qwen3.5 9B scores higher on SWE-bench Verified, but Mellum2.1 activates only 2.5B parameters per token. As a result, it generates tokens about 1.4x faster than Qwen3.5 9B for a single request and about 1.8x faster under load, as shown in our October post.

## How we trained it

Mellum2.1 Instruct went through the same two reinforcement learning stages as Thinking. First, it learned to solve standalone tasks in code, math, tool use, and instruction following. Then it learned to work as an agent in real repositories, using shell and file tools inside a sandbox and being rewarded only when the hidden tests passed.

We made two adjustments for Instruct. We tuned the length penalty for a model that answers without thinking, which keeps its answers concise and reduces the number of tokens without sacrificing quality. We also brought generation and training into closer agreement, which makes training more stable.

Both stages are built on NVIDIA NeMo open-source training libraries. NeMo RL, a post-training library, runs generation and training asynchronously, and NeMo Megatron-Bridge handles the weight updates across the large-scale distributed clusters of NVIDIA H200 and B300 GPUs. Together they let a single run collect about half a million agent trajectories from 10,000 concurrent sandboxes.

This release builds on open research, frameworks, and datasets. That is why Mellum2.1 is also open for others to build on.

...

Both variants of Mellum2.1 are available on Hugging Face under Apache 2.0. Each one also comes in two additional versions:

- GGUF files for running the model on your own machine (Instruct, Thinking).
- A multi-token prediction (MTP) head that makes generation up to 1.8x faster (Instruct, Thinking).

signals.title: vLLM engineers report faster prefill and agent-tuned kernels | AI.info
signals.excerpt:
Prefill processes input tokens before a model begins generating its response. In the prefill test, a two-stage pipeline-parallel setup, PP2, was compared with TEP2 plus sequence parallelism using MiniMax-M3.1-Flash on two GB300 GPUs.

Inferact’s Thien Tran, a member of technical staff, described several changes to the pipeline approach: balancing stages by measured time rather than layer count, limiting step size and moving activation transfers onto copy engines. The transfer change cut median time to first token by 13–20% near saturation, according to the team, and is now enabled by default on NVLink.

With fixed step sizes, the comparison layout remained faster at a tight time-to-first-token target of 0.75 seconds, while PP2 led at looser targets. A new scheduler sizes each micro-batch from the queue; the team says it matched the best hand-tuned step size without tuning and put PP2 ahead from about 0.5 seconds upward.

...

Inferact’s Ao Shen, a member of technical staff, presented work with NVIDIA DevTech and NVIDIA Research on matching kernels used for reinforcement-learning rollout and training. The two can split the same floating-point sum differently, causing their results to drift apart.

The team used an agent loop that first makes each layer match bit for bit, then substitutes faster kernels and checks that the difference remains zero. It says the approach brought the cost of exact kernels down to about 10% of rollout speed. The open-source skill worked on Nemotron, DeepSeek V4.1 and Kimi K3.1, the team reports.

With the exact kernels, the REINFORCE Zero approach reweights every token. In the reported comparison, it reached 48.80% accuracy against 48.91% for synchronous reinforcement learning, while reducing time per update from 49.4 seconds to 20.6 seconds.

signals.excerpt:
## New Agent Framework Facilitates Biological Database Retrieval and Integration

Date: 2026-11-25 Source: Chinese Academy of Sciences

Biological research questions often span multiple bioinformatics databases, which differ in data structures, access interfaces and coverage. To retrieve and integrate data across databases, researchers need to select suitable sources and call the corresponding query interfaces.

Interpreting the results requires consideration of species information, entity relationships and evidence from the literature. Building these steps into a natural-language query application also requires connecting database interfaces, writing assistant instructions and defining how information passes between query steps, making the process tedious and complex to implement.

Recently, the National Genomics Data Center, as part of the Beijing Institute of Genomics (China National Center for Bioinformation), has developed and released Dingent, a configurable agent framework. The framework integrates data-access plugins, assistant configurations, directed workflows and model configurations, and provides a configuration interface for building agent applications.

The work "Dingent: a configurable agent framework for biological database retrieval and integration", was published online in Computational and Structural Biotechnology on November 18.

To evaluate the retrieval performance and operational characteristics of the Dingent agent framework, the research team constructed 55 questions using fixed data snapshots from the integrated canine multi-omics resource iDog and the biomarker knowledge base BioKA. The questions covered six task categories: exact matching, single-attribute filtering, condition combinations, cross-table joins, missing information and synonym understanding.

Dingent was compared with a single-assistant baseline that supported tool calling. Each system answered each question three times, producing 330 outputs in total.

Two reviewers independently scored the outputs under blinded conditions. The fully correct rates were 60.00% for Dingent and 63.03% for the single-assistant baseline. The difference was −3.03 percentage points (95% confidence interval: −13.94 to 8.48, based on paired comparison).

The study also recorded query latency, model calls and token usage for both systems under their respective execution settings, providing experimental data for analyzing retrieval performance and resource consumption. These measurements also provide a reference for future evaluations of more complex, multi-step biological tasks under uniform, controlled conditions.

Researchers then used iDog and BioKA to illustrate how cross-resource queries can be configured. In the example, the workflow retrieves genes associated with canine degenerative myelopathy from iDog, then uses the returned SOD1 and SP110 gene identifiers to query related records in BioKA.

Dingent's source code, plugin repository and documentation are publicly available, enabling research teams to configure natural-language retrieval applications for their own databases. The study's supplementary materials provide database snapshots, evaluation questions, query results, human ratings and analysis code to support verification and reproducibility.
